Equip AI with “Gear,” Not Just “Intelligence”: OpenAI’s “Agent Skills” Breaks the Spell of Prompting “How many times do I have to hammer the same instructions into the AI?”
Every engineer has likely let out a sigh of frustration in front of their screen at some point. No matter how smart a Large Language Model (LLM) is, it often forgets context or requires you to explain everything from scratch. Are we, without realizing it, becoming exhausted “educators” for our AI agent “subordinates”?
However, those unproductive hours might finally be coming to an end. OpenAI has been quietly but steadily developing a repository called “skills.” This repository suggests a paradigm shift: moving away from an era where AI reads prompts toward an era where we “equip AI with skills.”
The tech media outlet “White Onion Tech” dives deep into the true nature of this revolution.
The End of Prompt Engineering, the Birth of Agent Plugins If you were to describe OpenAI’s “skills” in one sentence, it would be: “An external brain and expansion module for AI.”
Until now, making an AI behave in a specific way required chanting “incantations” in the form of system prompts thousands of characters long. However, this repository proposes a philosophy deeply rooted in software engineering: “Write once, use everywhere.”
Procedures the AI should execute, necessary scripts, and resources are defined as a single “package (skill).” The AI then discovers these skills on its own and “installs” them as its own functions as needed. This worldview mirrors the scenes in the sci-fi movie The Matrix, where programs are uploaded directly into the brain. It’s hard not to get excited.
Three “Vital Points” Stimulating Intellectual Curiosity Why does “skills” hold value beyond being just another library? The reason lies in three core features:
“Encapsulation” of Skills: Instructions and execution code are sealed within a single folder. This dramatically improves logic reusability. You no longer need to copy and paste similar prompts across different projects. The Magic Command $skill-installer: In a Codex environment, this single command allows you to mount new abilities onto the AI. You can expand the AI’s functionality on demand, much like installing a plugin. Breaking Free from “Platforms”: This is the most crucial point. It is based on a standard specification (agentskills.io) designed to share and distribute “skills” across the entire industry, regardless of the specific platform. In other words, this isn’t a closed experiment by OpenAI alone; it aims to be a common language for the entire AI ecosystem. Just Seconds: The Moment AI Meets its “New Self” The implementation is almost surprisingly simple. For instance, suppose you want to give an AI the ability to comment on GitHub pull requests. All you have to do is issue a single-line command:
$skill-installer gh-address-comments Furthermore, if you want to try experimental features that no one else has accessed yet, you can simply point directly to the repository URL:
$skill-installer install https://github.com/openai/skills/tree/main/skills/.experimental/create-plan With just this, an AI that was merely a “knowledgeable chatbot” yesterday transforms into an “agent that autonomously formulates and executes plans” today. This tangible sense of progression is exactly what stirs a developer’s soul.
What Do We Gain from This Technology? Imagine a future where, instead of explaining to a new team member, “Read this document to learn the conventions of this repository,” you simply have them run $skill-installer project-standard. Or a world where complex deployment flows aren’t controlled by finicky prompts, but are defined as a single “skill” for the AI to complete.
What lies there isn’t the struggle of “coaxing an AI to work,” but the inherent intellectual excitement of an engineer: “combining high-level parts to construct the ultimate automation mechanism.”
Expectations and a Sane Perspective Of course, it’s not all sunshine and roses.
Pros: Liberation from the “secret sauce” hell of managing prompts. Overwhelming speed generated by skill portability. Cons: Currently, it is heavily dependent on the Codex environment, and it will likely take time for integration with other LLMs and the maturity of the ecosystem. However, the fact that OpenAI has moved toward “standardization” is significant. They are trying to turn “execution power”—which lies beyond “intelligence”—into a package that anyone can handle.

Current common sense regarding copyright might be literally “turned upside down”—a shockwave that is currently rocking the tech industry.
The tech giant Meta has taken the bold stance in court that “even the act of uploading pirated e-books via BitTorrent constitutes ‘fair use’ as long as it is for AI training.”

The Forbidden Fruit called “Books3”: The “Books3” dataset, which Meta allegedly used to train Llama, contains tens of thousands of pirated books. While authors have sued, calling this a “clear copyright infringement,” Meta shows no signs of backing down. Logic that Justifies Even “Uploading”: Normally, sharing pirated content is an automatic violation. However, Meta argues that the process of training an AI model to create “new value (intelligence)” constitutes “Transformative Use,” which is distinct from simply reading the original book. In other words, their logic is that if the purpose is noble, the act of uploading during that process can be justified. Defining BitTorrent as “Just Efficiency”: For Meta, using P2P networks to acquire data is merely an “efficient means of data collection.” It is an ultra-aggressive stance that seeks to overwrite existing legal frameworks with the speed of the AI era. 🔥 🔧 Why Engineers Should Watch This “Quagmire” This isn’t just a dispute for legal departments. It is a vital issue directly linked to the front lines of development.
Determining the “Purity” of Training Data:
Until now, engineers in Japan have been protected by the shield of Article 30-4 of the Copyright Act. However, if Meta’s argument prevails in the U.S., the global “legal line” for data usage will be significantly lowered. This would mean the degree of freedom in the data we can access will expand explosively. The “Right to Exist” for OSS Models:
If open-source models like Llama are certified as “legally clean,” a golden age of OSS models that both companies and individuals can use with peace of mind will arrive. Escape the Labyrinth of 0s and 1s: Visualizing the “AI Mind” with Iris Classification—A Weapon for Python Beginners Introduction: Why “Iris,” and Why Now? “I want to dive into AI and machine learning, but I’m not ready to drown in a storm of mathematical formulas.” If that sounds like you, you’re on the right track. What we seek isn’t math for the sake of academia, but the “wisdom” to solve real-world problems.
To find that wisdom, we must return to the birthplace of data scientists worldwide: the “Iris Classification” dataset. Why is plant data from nearly 100 years ago still so beloved today? It’s because this tiny flower contains the entire essence of machine learning.
In this post, we’ll explore the excitement of building an intelligent model in Python using Decision Trees—an algorithm that strips away the mystery and lays the AI’s decision-making process bare.
Decision Trees: A Lens into the “AI Brain” While many AI models tend to be “black boxes,” Decision Trees are different. This algorithm is profoundly human-centric.
A Stack of “If-Then” Logic: It translates human-like decision-making—such as “If the petal width is 0.8cm or less, it’s a Setosa”—directly into logic. No Need for Data “Hand-Holding”: It’s incredibly robust. You can get solid results without the tedious work of numerical normalization or standardization. The Satisfaction of Visualization: When you output the results as a tree diagram, you gain a perfect understanding of the logic the AI used to reach its conclusion. Think of a Decision Tree as a “butler of peak logical thinking.” Let’s experience its faithful service through code.
Just a Few Lines: The Ritual of Implementing “Intelligence” Using Python’s crown jewel, scikit-learn, machine learning is no longer a form of dark magic. With just these few lines, a computer learns how to distinguish between species of Iris.
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split # Loading data: Load the "4 features" of 150 samples iris = load_iris() X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(iris.data, iris.target, random_state=42) # Building and training the model: Limiting tree depth to "3" to create an elegant and smart decision boundary clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3) clf.fit(X_train, y_train) # Accuracy check: How well can it predict unknown data? print(f"Accuracy: {clf.score(X_test, y_test):.2f}") How Decision Trees Change Your Perspective This simple algorithm isn’t just for classifying flowers; its applications are vast.
A Compass for Marketing: You can perform human-centric analysis, such as identifying that “Users over 30 who access the site on weekends have a higher conversion rate.” Predictive Maintenance: If a sensor exceeds a certain value while an abnormal noise is detected, it’s a “failure.” You can convert the “intuition” of veteran technicians into a digital asset. Light and Shadow: The Fragility of Decision Trees Of course, it isn’t an omnipotent god. Decision Trees have a trap called “Overfitting,” where they become too obsessed with specific data points. If the tree grows too deep, it stops being a “law” and degrades into “mere rote memorization.” This is why engineers must hold the “reins”—the max_depth parameter—to keep the AI’s logic from running wild.

The End of the “Proton Myth”? Why We Shouldn’t Overestimate Anonymity: Lessons from FBI Cooperation “If you use Proton Mail, even state authorities can’t touch you.” For those of us who believed in this kind of digital Eden, the recent news must have felt like a bucket of cold water to the face.
The FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) identified and arrested an Atlanta protester using information provided by Proton Mail. This report has even triggered cries of “betrayal” among privacy-conscious engineers and activists.
However, before we pivot to emotional criticism, we need to look at the facts calmly. Why did an “identity exposure” happen with Proton, a service touted as the ultimate shield? What we find isn’t a flaw in the tool itself, but a pitfall called “lax operational security.” By the end of this article, you will understand the true nature of anonymity and the essence of the “digital self-defense” you should review starting tomorrow.
The Vault Remains Unbroken—But the “Footprints” Were Real First, let’s clear up a misunderstanding. Proton’s vaunted “End-to-End Encryption (E2EE)” was not breached, and the contents of the emails were not read. The vault door remained tightly shut. So, how did the FBI reach the suspect?
The reasons are ironically simple, and there are three of them:
The “Backdoor” of Recovery Addresses: The biggest fatal error in this case was linking a personal “Gmail” address as a recovery email for the Proton account. When Proton received a Swiss court order, they disclosed this recovery address, which allowed authorities to identify the individual through the linked Google account. Fingerprints Known as “Metadata”: Even if the content cannot be read, records of “when, who, and which address someone communicated with” (metadata) can be subject to disclosure under legal compulsion. Think of it this way: the contents of the letter were invisible, but the writing on the envelope was recorded. The Illusion that “Switzerland is Safe”: While Proton is based in Switzerland, if an act is considered a “crime” under Swiss law, the company is obligated to provide information through local authorities. Switzerland may be a neutral country, but it is not a lawless zone. 3 Ironclad Rules for Protecting Privacy That Every Engineer Should Know Blind trust in a tool—the “I’m safe because I use X” mindset—is the most dangerous vulnerability for an engineer. Here is how you should integrate these lessons into your own OpSec (Operational Security).
Avoid the Fatal Wound of “Linking”: If you want to maximize anonymity, registering a daily-use email as a recovery address is out of the question. You should use a burner email service or consider the option of “not setting one at all,” while accepting the risk of losing access. Use VPNs and Tor Like You Breathe: Hide even the IP address used to connect to Proton. This is the baseline. As Proton itself recommends, unless you obfuscate your connection path, no encrypted email can escape physical tracking of “where it was sent from.” Evade the SMS Authentication Trap: The moment a service asks for a phone number during registration, it links to your physical identity. Choose services that do not require a phone number whenever possible. If one is required, consider a high-anonymity SIM. That level of commitment is what “anonymity” actually requires. Even So, There Is No Need to Abandon Proton Mail If you ask, “So, is Proton ultimately no different from Gmail?” the answer is a resounding “NO.”
Even the FBI, one of the world’s most powerful investigative agencies, could not decrypt the “content of the emails” themselves. This fact proves that Proton’s encryption technology remains robust. What was exposed here was not the limit of the tool, but rather the “boundary of literacy” regarding user privacy.
In the end, perhaps we are asking too much magic from our tools. No matter how sharp the sword, it will harm the wielder if they are unskilled.

Conclusion: Anonymity is Defined by “Tool × Operation” Proton Mail is a “top-tier component” for protecting privacy, but it does not make you invisible on its own. In cases where state power truly moves, there is no service in this world that can completely transcend the walls of law and physics.
If you wish to remain anonymous, you must constantly be aware of where and how much of your digital footprint remains, and continue to question it. Only the accumulation of that meticulous, unglamorous operation will truly protect you.
Now that you’ve finished this article, please review your account settings once more. Are you hiding the key to your vault under a welcome mat named “Google”? 🔥

Ending “Environment Pollution” in JupyterLab: The Fastest Way to Boost Development Clarity by Adding Virtual Environments as Kernels You added a single library, and suddenly the code that worked perfectly yesterday starts throwing a tantrum. Or perhaps you’re staring at the red “ModuleNotFoundError” text in Jupyter, looking up at the ceiling and sighing, “But I just installed it…”
Does this sound familiar? If you are stuffing every library into JupyterLab’s base environment, you are essentially over-simmering a “secret sauce” until the pot becomes an unrecognizable mess.
The key to unlocking the true power of JupyterLab lies in a simple habit: “Registering virtual environments as independent kernels.” By the time you finish reading this article, your development environment will have the clarity of a fog that has finally lifted.
💡 Why “Environment Isolation” is a Critical Issue Right Now The modern world of AI and Data Science is, in a sense, a “Warring States period” for libraries. Updates happen at a staggering pace, and “dependency conflicts”—where the latest library for one project breaks the lifeline of another—are a daily occurrence.
Environment Sanctification: Building an “isolated clean room” (virtual environment) for each project is a minimum requirement for professional work. Trust via Reproducibility: Graduate from the “it works on my machine” excuse and ensure your code runs in anyone’s environment. The Aesthetic of Switching: Switching kernels with a single click in the GUI. That instant transition creates a rhythm for the engineer. 🔧 The 3-Step Ritual: Taming Virtual Environments as “Kernels” The procedure is surprisingly simple. However, these few lines of command will save you hours of frustration. We’ll use the standard venv as an example to walk through the steps.
1. Constructing the Sanctuary (Virtual Environment) It begins by creating a dedicated sandbox for your project.
# Summon the virtual environment "my_env" python -m venv my_env # Enter the sanctuary (Mac/Linux) source my_env/bin/activate # For Windows # .\my_env\Scripts\activate 2. Inviting the Interpreter (ipykernel) This is the most important “missing link.” Simply creating a virtual environment isn’t enough; JupyterLab doesn’t know it exists yet. You need to install an “interpreter” inside the virtual environment to communicate with Jupyter.
pip install ipykernel 3. “Resident Registration” in JupyterLab Finally, register this environment in JupyterLab’s management directory. You are essentially telling it, “Show up in the menu with this name.”
python -m ipykernel install --user --name=my_env --display-name="Python (My_Env)" That’s it. Try clicking the kernel name in the top-right corner of JupyterLab. You should see your proudly named “Python (My_Env)” listed there. ✨
🚀 Use Cases: When This Technique Really Shines This environment management proves its worth in “battlefield” situations like these:
LLM and PyTorch Experiments: When you want to try libraries with strict version requirements without breaking other projects. Team Deliverables: When you want to build the exact library configuration for a deliverable without mixing it with your cluttered local environment. Parallel Projects: When you need to smartly handle chaotic situations like “Project A is Python 3.9, but Project B is 3.11.” ✅ Benefits and a Bit of Housekeeping Benefits: Your base environment stays clean. You minimize the risk of your PC becoming unstable and gain peace of mind. Housekeeping: As virtual environments proliferate, they will eventually start eating up storage. When an environment has served its purpose, let it go with gratitude using jupyter kernelspec uninstall <env_name>. 👇 Recommended Services for Engineers 👇 🌐 Get your unique domain at “Onamae.com”. TechTrend Watch uses it too!
🏁 Conclusion: Stop Wasting Energy on the Base Environment If you think of JupyterLab as just a “notebook where you can write code,” you’re missing out. It is an “external brain” for engineers, capable of parallel processing by instantly switching between multiple brains (kernels).
Trying to do everything in the base environment is like trying to race on a circuit while dragging the handbrake. Hit the terminal right now and build your own “ultimate specialized environment.”
That single step will push your development efficiency into another dimension. Welcome to a smarter development experience. 💻✨
